programme.title: Imagine...
programme.desc: Marina Abramovic is the reigning queen of performance art. She invites Alan Yentob into her home, opens up her enormous personal archive and travels back to her birthplace, Belgrade. Her early, provocative work was once dismissed, but today thousands go to see her perform pieces that can last for weeks, even months at a time. By using just her own body and pushing her physical and psychological boundaries, she has become an international artistic superstar.

programme.title: Fred Dibnah's Industrial Age
programme.desc: Fred's fascinating journey through Britain's industrial past sees him tracing the development of the railways, from the first steam locomotive to the record-breaking Mallard. The excitement reminds him of his childhood days when locomotives used to roar past his bedroom window, and Fred gets his hands dirty stoking the boiler of a Black Five as he speeds through the Welsh countryside.

programme.title: Railways: The Making of a Nation
programme.desc: The railways changed what people ate, and the culinary tastes of the population. Moving produce around at speed was suddenly possible, and fresh meat, wet fish, dairy, fruit and vegetables were now widely available.

programme.title: The Good Life
programme.desc: Financial solvency finds Tom and Barbara with £10 to spare, and Tom makes an executive decision to spend it all on a loom.

programme.title: Yes, Prime Minister
programme.desc: Jim Hacker considers cancelling the Trident programme after discovering some interesting facts about the UK's defence system.

programme.title: Henry VIII: Patron or Plunderer?
programme.desc: King Henry VIII had a fascinating and enlightening relationship with art. He came to the throne as the renaissance swept across Europe, yet England's new King never lost sight of the medieval chivalry of his forefathers. Architectural historian Jonathan Foyle looks at the palaces, tapestries, music and paintings created in the King's name.

programme.title: Storyville
programme.desc: In an era of escalating censorship, librarians have found themselves on the front line of America's culture wars. Explore how they are risking their safety to defend free speech as book bans and censorship threaten democracy from within.

programme.title: Blood and Gold: The Making of Spain with Simon Sebag Montefiore
programme.desc: Simon explores the early years of the country, its emergence as the battleground of empires and its golden age under the Cordoba Caliphate.

programme.title: Fred Dibnah's Industrial Age
programme.desc: Fred moves on to the golden age of shipbuilding, examining the skills of engineers who turned Britain into one of the foremost manufacturing nations. He also visits the world's first production line in Suffolk.

programme.title: Railways: The Making of a Nation
programme.desc: Trains reflected class divisions with separate carriages for first, second and third class passengers. Yet, seen at the time, they were also bringing people physically closer together. In the early 1800s Britain was clearly divided between upper, middle and working classes. The trains gradually acted as a great catalyst, mixing the country up as people were travelling to regions and places for the first time.

programme.title: Tutankhamun: The Truth Uncovered
programme.desc: What killed King Tutankhamun? Ever since his spectacular tomb was discovered, the boy king has been the most famous pharaoh of all ancient Egypt. But his mysterious death, at just 19 years old, has never been explained. In this BBC One special, presenter Dallas Campbell reveals new scientific research and carries out unique experiments to get to the truth. For the first time, a virtual autopsy of Tut's mummified body reveals astonishing secrets about the pharaoh.

programme.title: Thatcher: A Very British Revolution
programme.desc: Mrs Thatcher's victory in the 1979 general election propels her into power as Britain's first female prime minister. On the steps of Downing Street she promises hope and harmony but her first two years are characterised by disruption and division.

programme.title: William Nicholson Remembers: Sweet as You Are
programme.desc: Acclaimed screenwriter William Nicholson looks back on the BBC drama he still considers one of his finest achievements, 1988's As Sweet as You Are.

programme.title: Screen Two
programme.desc: A college lecturer contracts HIV after having a brief affair with one of his students. The news threatens his marriage and family life.

programme.title: Ardal O'Hanlon: Tomb Raider
programme.desc: The story of a 1930s quest to find the origins of the earliest Irish men and women on the island of Ireland using archaeology. Ardal goes back to world-famous archaeological sites to see how Ireland had some of the most important finds in Europe.

programme.title: How to Get Ahead
programme.desc: Stephen Smith looks back at the Medieval Age to find out what it took to get ahead at the court of Richard II. Richard presided over the first truly sophisticated and artistic court in England. Painters, sculptors, poets, tailors, weavers and builders flocked to court to make their fortunes. But these were dangerous times. Being close to Richard brought many a courtier to a sticky end. Featuring David Tennant and Clarissa Dickson Wright.
